Hello, my name is Dr. Amy Letterberg, and I'm chair of the Georgia Commission of the Deaf or Hard of Hearing.
This commission is appointed by the governor and General Assembly to advise the state.
We supported the PSC's Georgia hearing aid dispatch program since its inception in 2007.
The program is critical to improving the lives of deaf and hard of hearing Georgians, and we thank the PSC for this work.
As you may know, Medicaid, Medicare, and most private insurance do not pay for hearing aids for adults.
Without this program, hearing aids would be unaffordable.
Most adults funded by the program have a bilateral severe or profound hearing loss.
This means they cannot understand speech without hearing aids and are at risk for being socially isolated without obtaining them.
For children, many families have high deductible private insurance that makes it difficult to pay for hearing aids for their children.
Without hearing aids, these children will not develop spoken language or read on time.
So this program is truly a godsend.
We wholeheartedly support the staff recommendations to award the contract to the Speech and Hearing Clinic at University of Georgia.
The clinic has an extensive history of serving low-income Georgians.
We have the utmost respect for Dr. Alison Morrison, the audiologist who would lead the program at UGA.
She has a proven track record of improving access for hearing technology.
For example, she successfully led a statewide effort to change Medicaid reimbursement rules for children.
These changes remove barriers for young children receiving timely audiological care.
She tried to get a similar change for adult Medicaid patients, but that effort was unsuccessful.
I respectfully submit that one key factor in the award decision should be an evaluation of the performance of the Georgia Charitable Care Network, who currently has the contract.
The previous administrator, Georgia Lions Lighthouse, dispensed 1,795 hearing aids to 949 people in 2019.
That's the last year that they had a full year of the program.
In contrast, according to PSC staff, GCCN dispensed only 632 hearing aids in 2025.
In other words, by 2025, hearing aids dispensed by GCCN had fallen to just 35% of Lions Lighthouse.
Because 90% of people received two hearing aids, my estimate is that fewer than 350 people received hearing aids last year from GCCN.
This means that hundreds of Georgians did not receive the hearing aids they needed.
We have evidence that has been already testified here that this drop reflects issues of how the program had been administered.
There's not been a collapse in the number of Georgians eligible for these hearing aids.
Distributing hearing aids is a complex endeavor requiring knowledge of both hearing aid devices and audiological clinics.
That's why UGA's extensive contacts with the community should improve the administration of this program.
